lessons.title: IPv6 Addressing and Deployment
concepts: 128-bit hex: 2001:db8::/32; compression rules (:: once, leading zeros dropped); link-local fe80::/10, unique local fc00::/7, global unicast 2000::/3.
SLAAC (router advertisements) vs DHCPv6 (stateful/stateless); EUI-64 vs privacy extensions for interface IDs.
No NAT needed (enough addresses); neighbor discovery replaces ARP; OSPFv3/EIGRP named mode for routing.
Dual-stack transition; tunneling (6to4, Teredo legacy); 'IPv6-only with NAT64' for new builds.

example.code:
R1(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:db8:1::1/64
R1(config-if)# ipv6 nd prefix default no-autoconfig   ! DHCPv6 only
R1(config)# ipv6 router ospf 1
R1(config-rtr)# router-id 1.1.1.1
example.walkthrough: Enable routing, address interfaces, choose SLAAC/DHCPv6 per segment. 'New deployment, avoid NAT' → IPv6 native.

pitfalls: Forgetting ipv6 unicast-routing — addresses configured but nothing routes.
:: used twice in one address — illegal; compress only the longest run once.
Assuming NAT66 like v4 — IPv6 restores end-to-end; filter with ACLs instead.
lessons.try_it: Dual-stack a lab segment and verify v6-only connectivity with ping.

lessons.title: OSPF: Link-State Routing
concepts: OSPF areas (backbone area 0 required); router ID (highest loopback/IP); neighbor via Hello (10s, dead 40s) on multicast 224.0.0.5.
DR/BDR elected on multi-access (highest priority, then RID) to limit adjacencies; point-to-point needs none.
States: Down→Init→2-Way→ExStart→Exchange→Loading→Full; network types must match for adjacency.
Costs = reference bandwidth/interface BW (default 100 Mbps → cost 1 for FE+); LSA types 1/2/3/5; ABR between areas, ASBR to external.

example.code:
R1(config)# router ospf 1
R1(config-router)# router-id 1.1.1.1
R1(config-router)# network 10.0.0.0 0.255.255.255 area 0
R1(config-router)# passive-interface default
R1(config-router)# no passive-interface gi0/0
! verify: show ip ospf neighbor  |  show ip route ospf
example.walkthrough: Router ID, networks in areas, passive everywhere except real neighbors. 'Scale routing beyond statics' → single-area OSPF, then multi-area.

pitfalls: Area 0 discontiguous — all areas must touch backbone (or virtual-link).
Mismatched Hello/dead timers or area types — neighbors stuck in Init/ExStart.
Advertising too broadly (0.0.0.0/0 area 0) — be precise with network statements + passive interfaces.
lessons.try_it: Break an OSPF neighbor by mismatching MTU and diagnose via neighbor states.

lessons.title: NAT and PAT: Address Translation
concepts: Static NAT: 1:1 (server publishing); Dynamic NAT: pool 1:1; PAT (overload): many:1 via port multiplexing — the SOHO/branch standard.
Inside/outside designations on interfaces; NAT order: inside→outside checked against ACL/pool.
PAT table = (inside local IP:port ↔ outside global IP:port); 65k ports per global IP bound concurrent sessions.
NAT64/DNAT for v6→v4; double NAT when ISP also translates (CGNAT).

example.code:
R1(config)# ip nat inside source list 10 interface gi0/0 overload
R1(config)# access-list 10 permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255
R1(config-if)# ip nat inside    ! on LAN interface
R1(config-if)# ip nat outside   ! on WAN interface
! server publish: ip nat inside source static tcp 192.168.1.10 80 203.0.113.5 80
example.walkthrough: ACL defines who translates; overload multiplexes ports. 'Branch internet access, one public IP' → PAT overload.

pitfalls: Inside/outside swapped — translation never triggers.
PAT pool exhaustion — too few global IPs for session count; add addresses.
Static NAT without firewall rules — translation ≠ permission; ACLs still needed.
lessons.try_it: Show ip nat translations during a browsing session and map ports to flows.

lessons.title: ACLs: Standard, Extended, and Named
concepts: Standard (1-99, 1300-1999): source IP only — place near destination. Extended (100-199, 2000-2699): source/dest/protocol/port — place near source.
Implicit deny all at the end; top-down first-match; 'established' for return TCP; log keyword for hits.
Directions: inbound (before routing) vs outbound; VTY ACLs protect management access (access-class).
Named ACLs allow editing (sequence numbers); time-based ACLs for business-hours rules.

example.code:
ip access-list extended BLOCK-GUEST
 10 deny ip 192.168.99.0 0.0.0.255 10.0.0.0 0.255.255.255
 20 permit tcp 192.168.99.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 80
 30 permit tcp 192.168.99.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 443
interface gi0/1
 ip access-group BLOCK-GUEST in
example.walkthrough: Deny guest→internal, permit web only. 'Filter near source with ports' → extended ACL inbound on the source interface.

pitfalls: Standard ACL near source — blocks too broadly; standards go near destination.
Forgetting implicit deny — 'permit' lines only, then wonder why nothing works.
No established rule for return traffic — stateless ACLs need explicit return permits.
lessons.try_it: Write an extended ACL blocking Telnet everywhere but allowing SSH from admin net.

lessons.title: WAN Technologies: MPLS, MetroE, and SD-WAN
concepts: Leased lines (private, expensive), MPLS L3VPN (provider-routed, QoS, any-to-any), Metro Ethernet (E-Line/E-LAN, simple L2).
Internet VPN (cheap, encrypted overlay) vs private WAN (SLA, costly) — hybrid is the norm.
SD-WAN (vManage/vEdge, Viptela): centralized policy, app-aware routing, zero-touch, transport-independent — the modern answer.
Last-mile diversity (fiber + LTE) + dual transports = resilient branches.

example.code:
! SD-WAN policy: voice prefers MPLS, bulk prefers internet
policy
 app-route-policy VOICE-POLICY
  sequence 1
   match dscp 46
   action sla-class VOICE strict
    preferred-color mpls
example.walkthrough: App-aware path selection per SLA. 'Cut MPLS costs, keep voice quality' → SD-WAN with app policies.

pitfalls: Single transport to branches — no resilience; dual transports minimum.
MPLS everywhere by default — internet + SD-WAN often meets the SLA cheaper.
Ignoring underlay MTU with overlays — fragmentation kills performance.
lessons.try_it: Define an SD-WAN policy preferring MPLS for voice, internet for bulk.

lessons.title: Site-to-Site IPsec VPN
concepts: IKE Phase 1 (ISAKMP SA: encryption/auth/DH) → Phase 2 (IPsec SA: ESP/AH, transform sets); tunnel vs transport mode.
Crypto map (legacy) vs IPsec profiles with GRE/VTI: VTI gives a routable tunnel interface — preferred for dynamic routing.
Interesting traffic (crypto ACL) triggers the tunnel; PFS adds DH per rekey; DPD detects dead peers.
DMVPN for hub-spoke scale (mGRE + NHRP + IPsec); FlexVPN unifies with IKEv2.

example.code:
crypto ikev2 proposal PROP
 encryption aes-gcm-256
 integrity sha256
 group 20
crypto ikev2 policy POL
 proposal PROP
! VTI:
interface Tunnel0
 ip address 10.255.0.1 255.255.255.252
 tunnel source gi0/0
 tunnel destination 203.0.113.2
 tunnel protection ipsec profile PROF
example.walkthrough: IKEv2 proposal → policy → VTI with IPsec profile. VTI + routing protocol = dynamic failover, the modern answer over crypto maps.

pitfalls: Mismatched Phase 1/2 parameters — tunnel never completes; debugs show MM_NO_STATE/QM_IDLE.
Crypto ACL asymmetry — interesting traffic must mirror both ends.
No routing over crypto-map tunnels — use VTI/GRE for dynamic protocols.
lessons.try_it: Bring up a VTI tunnel and run OSPF across it.

lessons.title: First-Hop Redundancy: HSRP, VRRP, GLBP
concepts: HSRP (Cisco): active/standby routers share a virtual IP/MAC; hosts point at the VIP; preempt + priority decide roles; track interfaces to fail over.
VRRP: open standard, same concept (master/backup); GLBP: active load balancing across up to 4 routers via multiple virtual MACs.
Timers: hello 3s, hold 10s (HSRP default); authentication (plaintext/MD5) between peers.
VIP is the hosts' gateway — redundancy invisible to endpoints.

example.code:
R1(config-if)# standby 10 ip 192.168.1.1
R1(config-if)# standby 10 priority 110
R1(config-if)# standby 10 preempt
R1(config-if)# standby 10 track gi0/1 20   ! drop priority if uplink dies
example.walkthrough: Higher priority + preempt = deterministic active router; tracking ties failover to uplink health. 'Gateway redundancy' → HSRP/VRRP; 'gateway load balancing' → GLBP.

pitfalls: No preempt — a recovered better router never retakes active.
Forgetting to track the uplink — active router with dead WAN black-holes traffic.
HSRP in answer when question says multi-vendor — VRRP is the standard.
lessons.try_it: Fail the active router's uplink with tracking and watch sub-second failover.

lessons.title: QoS: Classification, Marking, and Queuing
concepts: Classification (ACL/NBAR) → marking (DSCP/IP precedence/CoS) → queuing (CBWFQ priority queue for voice) → policing/shaping.
Trust boundary: trust DSCP from phones, remark at access for PCs; EF (46) voice, AF classes for data.
Congestion management: LLQ (priority + CBWFQ) guarantees voice bandwidth; WRED drops TCP early to avoid tail-drop.
Shaping buffers/delays, policing drops/remarks — shape outbound, police inbound.

example.code:
class-map match-any VOICE
 match dscp ef
policy-map WAN-OUT
 class VOICE
  priority percent 30
 class CALL-SIGNALING
  bandwidth percent 5
 class class-default
  fair-queue
interface gi0/0
 service-policy output WAN-OUT
example.walkthrough: Voice gets strict priority (LLQ), signaling gets bandwidth, rest fair-queues. 'Choppy voice on congested WAN' → LLQ for EF.

pitfalls: Trusting PC markings — remark at the access edge; trust only phones.
Priority queue without policer — voice can starve everything; police it.
QoS on LAN without congestion — QoS only matters where queues form (WAN/uplinks).
lessons.try_it: Saturate a link with and without LLQ and compare voice MOS scores.

lessons.title: NTP, DNS, and SNMP Essentials
concepts: NTP stratum hierarchy (0 atomic → 1 → 2...); authentication optional; logs/certs/Kerberos all break on clock skew.
DNS: client resolver → recursive → root/TLD/authoritative; record types A/AAAA/CNAME/MX/PTR/TXT/SRV.
SNMP: v1/v2c (community strings, insecure) vs v3 (authPriv: auth + encryption); MIBs/OIDs polled or trapped.
Syslog levels 0-7 (emerg→debug); timestamps + NTP = correlatable logs.

example.code:
R1(config)# ntp server 10.0.0.1 prefer
R1(config)# ntp authenticate
R1(config)# ip name-server 8.8.8.8
R1(config)# snmp-server community READONLY RO
R1(config)# snmp-server host 10.0.0.50 version 3 priv netadmin
example.walkthrough: NTP first (everything depends on time), DNS for names, SNMPv3 for monitoring. 'Logs show wrong times' → NTP.

pitfalls: SNMPv2c on untrusted networks — community strings in cleartext; use v3 authPriv.
No NTP auth on critical infra — spoofed time breaks everything subtly.
DNS without fallback — one name-server is a single point of failure.
lessons.try_it: Break NTP and watch Kerberos/802.1X failures cascade.

lessons.title: Device Hardening and Management Security
concepts: Disable unused services (no ip http server, no cdp on edge... selectively), SSH only (crypto key, v2, ACL on VTY), strong passwords (secret > password, AES encryption).
AAA: TACACS+ (Cisco, per-command auth) vs RADIUS (open, combined auth) — centralize logins, accounting for audit.
Control plane policing (CoPP) rate-limits management traffic; disable Telnet, SNMPv1/2c write, finger.
Banner (legal warning), exec-timeout, logging buffered + syslog, NTP auth, config archive.

example.code:
hostname R1
ip domain-name corp.local
crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
ip ssh version 2
line vty 0 4
 transport input ssh
 access-class MGMT in
 exec-timeout 5 0
username admin privilege 15 secret $trong!
service password-encryption
example.walkthrough: SSHv2 + VTY ACL + timeout + strong secrets = the hardening baseline. 'Secure device management' → AAA + SSH + ACLs.

pitfalls: Telnet left enabled — credentials in cleartext; transport input ssh only.
Type-7 'encryption' treated as secure — it is reversible obfuscation; use secret (scrypt).
No VTY ACL — management reachable from anywhere.
lessons.try_it: Harden a router per the baseline and scan it from outside.

lessons.title: Network Automation: REST, NETCONF, and Python
concepts: RESTCONF/NETCONF use YANG models for structured config (vs screen-scraping CLI); REST APIs (DNA Center, Meraki, vManage) use JSON over HTTPS.
Python: Netmiko (SSH CLI automation), NAPALM (multi-vendor abstraction), ncclient (NETCONF), requests (REST).
Source of truth (NetBox) → templates (Jinja2) → deployment (Ansible) = the automation pipeline.
Idempotency: automation must be safely re-runnable; validate with pre/post checks.

example.code:
from netmiko import ConnectHandler
dev = ConnectHandler(device_type='cisco_ios', host='10.0.0.1',
                     username='netops', password='...')
out = dev.send_config_from_file('golden.cfg')
dev.save_config(); dev.disconnect()
# better: template + diff + commit via NAPALM
example.walkthrough: Template the config, diff against live, push if clean. Exam: 'automate 100 switches consistently' → Ansible + Jinja2 + NetBox.

pitfalls: Screen-scraping without error handling — one prompt change breaks everything; prefer structured APIs.
No config backups before automation — always archive first.
Pushing without diff/dry-run — automation amplifies mistakes at scale.
lessons.try_it: Render a Jinja2 interface template for 3 switches from one data file.

lessons.title: DNA Center and Intent-Based Networking
concepts: DNA Center: controller for campus — design (hierarchies), policy (SDA), provision (PnP/SWIM), assurance (health analytics).
SDA: underlay (IS-IS) + overlay (VXLAN/LISP) + policy (TrustSec/SGT) — macro/micro segmentation without VLAN sprawl.
PnP zero-touch provisioning; SWIM manages images; assurance uses telemetry for client/network health scores.
APIs (Intent APIs) let scripts drive DNA Center — automation on top of automation.

example.code:
# DNA Center Intent API: claim a device
POST /dna/intent/api/v1/onboarding/pnp-device/claim
{"deviceId": "...", "siteId": "...", "type": "Default"}
# then provision via template programmer
example.walkthrough: Design once → provision everywhere → assure continuously. 'Zero-touch branch rollout' → PnP + templates.

pitfalls: Treating DNA Center as monitoring-only — its value is closed-loop (design→provision→assure).
SDA without planning underlay MTU — VXLAN overhead needs 1550+ MTU.
Ignoring assurance baselines — deploy, then define 'healthy' thresholds.
lessons.try_it: Use the API to pull device health and build a simple dashboard.

lessons.title: VLANs: Segmentation at Layer 2
concepts: VLANs split one switch into multiple broadcast domains: VLAN 10 = Sales, VLAN 20 = Engineering — same hardware, isolated traffic.
Access ports carry one VLAN (untagged) for end hosts; trunk ports carry many (802.1Q tagged, native VLAN untagged).
Inter-VLAN routing needs a Layer-3 device: router-on-a-stick (subinterfaces) or SVIs on a multilayer switch (faster).
Voice VLANs separate phones (with QoS trust); default VLAN 1 should never carry user traffic.

example.code:
Switch(config)# vlan 10
Switch(config-vlan)# name SALES
Switch(config)# interface range fa0/1-12
Switch(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
Switch(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 10
Switch(config-if-range)# switchport voice vlan 150
example.walkthrough: Access ports → one VLAN; phones get voice VLAN + data VLAN on one port. 'Separate departments on one switch' → VLANs + trunk to router/SVI.

pitfalls: Forgetting inter-VLAN routing — VLANs alone cannot talk to each other.
Native VLAN mismatch on trunks — CDP warns, traffic for native VLAN leaks/misroutes.
Leaving all ports in VLAN 1 — security and broadcast-domain hygiene fail.
lessons.try_it: Create 3 VLANs, assign ports, and verify isolation with ping before adding routing.

lessons.title: Spanning Tree: Loop-Free Layer 2
concepts: STP (802.1D) blocks redundant links to prevent broadcast storms: elects root bridge (lowest BID = priority + MAC), then root/designated/blocking ports.
Port states: blocking → listening → learning → forwarding (30-50s convergence); RSTP (802.1w) converges in seconds via proposal/agreement.
PortFast skips STP on host ports (with BPDU Guard to shut down on loops); UplinkFast/BackboneFast are legacy RSTP predecessors.
Root Guard protects root placement; Loop Guard prevents unidirectional-link loops.

example.code:
Switch(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10 root primary
Switch(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10 root secondary   ! on backup
Switch(config-if)# spanning-tree portfast
Switch(config-if)# spanning-tree bpduguard enable
! verify: show spanning-tree vlan 10
example.walkthrough: Set root deterministically (lowest priority on core), PortFast+BPDU Guard on host ports. 'Converge faster' → RSTP/MST; 'host port slow' → PortFast.

pitfalls: Letting MAC addresses elect the root — oldest switch wins by accident; set priority explicitly.
PortFast on trunk/uplink ports — a loop forms with no STP protection; BPDU Guard mitigates.
PVST+ per-VLAN load balancing without planning — root placement per VLAN matters.
lessons.try_it: Break a redundant link and time RSTP convergence vs classic STP.

lessons.title: EtherChannel: Bundled Links
concepts: EtherChannel bonds 2-8 links into one logical link: more bandwidth + redundancy, STP sees one link (no blocking).
LACP (802.3ad, open) vs PAgP (Cisco): modes active/passive (LACP), desirable/auto (PAgP) — at least one side active/desirable.
All member links must match: speed, duplex, VLANs, trunking — mismatches break the bundle.
Load balances by hash (src/dst MAC or IP); single flow never exceeds one member's bandwidth.

example.code:
Switch(config)# interface range gi0/1-2
Switch(config-if-range)# channel-group 1 mode active
Switch(config)# interface port-channel 1
Switch(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
Switch(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20
example.walkthrough: LACP active both ends, configure the port-channel interface (it propagates to members). 'More bandwidth + redundancy between switches' → EtherChannel.

pitfalls: Mismatched parameters across members — bundle never forms; check speed/duplex/VLANs.
Both sides passive/auto — no negotiation happens; one side must initiate.
Expecting one flow to use combined bandwidth — hashing pins flows to single links.
lessons.try_it: Bundle 2 links with LACP, shut one member, and verify zero STP reconvergence.

lessons.title: SD-Access: Campus Fabric
concepts: SD-Access overlays a campus fabric on the underlay: LISP for control plane, VXLAN for data plane, TrustSec/SGT for segmentation.
Fabric roles: edge nodes (APs/users), border nodes (to outside), control-plane nodes (LISP map server), WLC integrated.
DNA Center automates: underlay, overlay, policy (SGT), host tracking — CLI becomes the exception.
Micro-segmentation via SGTs replaces VLAN-sprawl ACLs: policy follows the user, not the port.

example.code:
! Underlay: IS-IS or OSPF; overlay auto-provisioned by DNA Center
! Policy example (DNA Center):
! SGT 10 (Employees) -> SGT 20 (Printers): permit
! SGT 10 (Employees) -> SGT 30 (IoT): deny
example.walkthrough: DNA Center discovers, provisions underlay + fabric, policy in SGTs. 'Segmentation without VLAN sprawl' → SD-Access.

pitfalls: Designing like a legacy campus — the fabric abstracts L2; think in policies.
Underlay MTU — VXLAN overhead needs jumbo MTU end to end.
Skipping DNA Center — manual fabric config defeats the purpose.
lessons.try_it: Map a user-to-printer policy from VLANs to SGTs.

lessons.title: VRRP and GLBP in Practice
concepts: VRRP: open-standard master/backup, virtual MAC 0000.5e00.01xx; preempt by default (unlike HSRP).
GLBP: one AVG assigns virtual MACs to AVFs — active-active forwarding across up to 4 routers.
GLBP weighting + tracking: shift load away from degraded routers automatically.
Choose: HSRP (Cisco shops), VRRP (multi-vendor), GLBP (need load balancing).

example.code:
! GLBP: load-balanced gateway
interface Gi0/0
 glbp 10 ip 10.1.0.1
 glbp 10 priority 110
 glbp 10 preempt
 glbp 10 weighting 100 lower 80
 glbp 10 weighting track 1 decrement 30
example.walkthrough: AVG hands out different virtual MACs — hosts ARP to different forwarders. 'Use both uplinks for gateway traffic' → GLBP.

pitfalls: VRRP preempt surprises — it preempts by default; plan priority accordingly.
GLBP without weighting track — degraded router keeps full load.
Mixing FHRP protocols on one segment — pick one.
lessons.try_it: Verify hosts resolve to different AVF MACs under GLBP.

lessons.title: EtherChannel: Advanced Design
concepts: LACP (802.3ad, active/passive) negotiates; PAgP is Cisco-proprietary; 'on' forces without negotiation.
Load balancing: hash of src/dst IP+MAC+port — one flow uses one link; more entropy = better spread.
Min-links: bundle fails below threshold; max-bundle caps members; LACP system priority decides standby.
Layer 3 EtherChannels route; cross-stack (StackWise/VSS/vPC) for chassis redundancy.

example.code:
interface range Gi1/0/1-2
 channel-group 10 mode active
!
interface Port-channel10
 switchport mode trunk
!
port-channel load-balance src-dst-ip
example.walkthrough: LACP active both ends; tune the hash for your traffic mix. 'One elephant flow on one link' → expected; hashing is per-flow.

pitfalls: Mode 'on' one side, LACP other — bundle never forms cleanly.
Default MAC hash with routed traffic — src-dst-ip spreads better.
Members with mismatched config — speed/duplex/VLAN must match.
lessons.try_it: Show the hash result for test flows and rebalance if skewed.

lessons.title: OSI and TCP/IP: The Layered Models
concepts: OSI 7 layers: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application — 'Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away.' TCP/IP merges to 4: Link, Internet, Transport, Application.
Encapsulation: each layer adds its header (L2 frame, L3 packet, L4 segment); decapsulation strips on receipt. Devices: hub=L1, switch=L2, router=L3.
Data units: bits (L1), frames (L2, MAC), packets (L3, IP), segments (L4 TCP) / datagrams (UDP). Exam loves asking which PDU at which layer.
Troubleshooting top-down vs bottom-up: physical first (link lights, cables) eliminates half the possibilities immediately.

example.code:
L7-5  HTTP GET /index.html
L4   TCP  src:49152 dst:80  seq=1000
L3   IP   src:192.168.1.10 dst:93.184.216.34
L2   ETH  src:aaaa.bbbb.cccc dst:dddd.eeee.ffff
L1   bits on wire

Switch reads L2 only. Router strips L2, reads L3, re-encapsulates.
example.walkthrough: Draw the stack and label which device reads which layer. 'Which layer does a switch operate at?' → L2, reads MACs only.

pitfalls: Saying routers read MAC addresses for forwarding — routers route on IP (L3), rewriting L2 each hop.
Mixing PDU names — frame=L2, packet=L3, segment=L4 TCP.
Starting troubleshooting at L7 — always verify L1/L2 (link, duplex) first.
lessons.try_it: Capture with Wireshark and label each layer's header in one packet.

lessons.title: Subnetting: Masks, CIDR, and Address Math
concepts: Subnet mask splits host bits: /24 = 256 addresses (254 usable); usable = 2^hostbits − 2 (network + broadcast reserved).
Magic number = 256 − interesting octet: subnets increment by it. /26 → magic 64 → subnets .0, .64, .128, .192 with 62 hosts each.
VLSM: right-size each subnet (point-to-point /30 or /31, VLAN /26) to stop wasting addresses — required for efficient designs.

example.code:
Need: 4 LANs (50 hosts each) + 3 WAN links
VLANs: /26 (62 hosts) x4 -> 192.168.1.0/26, .64/26, .128/26, .192/26
WANs: /30 (2 hosts) x3 -> 192.168.2.0/30, .4/30, .8/30
Summary: 192.168.0.0/21 covers all (or summarize per site)
example.walkthrough: Largest requirement first, then fill. Exam shortcut: memorize /30=2, /29=6, /28=14, /27=30, /26=62, /25=126, /24=254 usable hosts.

pitfalls: Forgetting to subtract network + broadcast — /26 has 62 usable, not 64.
Overlapping VLSM allocations — allocate sequentially from the largest block down.
Using public IPs internally when RFC1918 suffices — exam designs always use private.
lessons.try_it: Subnet 172.16.0.0/16 into 8 equal LANs and 4 /30 WANs in under 5 minutes.

lessons.title: VLSM and Route Summarization
concepts: VLSM lets different masks in one network; summarization ( supernetting ) advertises one route for many — smaller tables, faster convergence.
Summarize at distribution/core boundaries; the summary must cover all specifics with the longest mask that still includes them all.
Summary drawback: black-holing if a component subnet is down — null0 discard routes and careful design mitigate.
Binary method: find common high-order bits; the summary mask = number of common bits.

example.walkthrough: Four /24s → one /22. Fewer LSAs, faster SPF. Exam: 'reduce routing table size' → summarize at boundaries.

pitfalls: Summarizing discontiguous networks — summary must be contiguous to be valid.
Over-summarizing past the common bits — includes foreign networks, misroutes traffic.
Forgetting summaries hide topology changes — troubleshooting needs the specifics.
lessons.try_it: Summarize 10.1.0.0/24 through 10.1.7.0/24 into the longest valid summary.

lessons.title: DHCPv6 and SLAAC
concepts: SLAAC: routers advertise prefixes (RA), hosts self-configure — no DHCP needed for addressing.
DHCPv6: stateful (addresses) or stateless (DNS only, with SLAAC); M/O flags in RA control the mix.
DUID (not MAC) identifies clients; relay agents forward across routers.
Common: SLAAC + stateless DHCPv6 for DNS — simple and robust.

example.code:
interface Gi0/0
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:1::1/64
 ipv6 nd other-config-flag        ! O=1: stateless DHCPv6 for DNS
 ipv6 dhcp server POOL rapid-commit
example.walkthrough: RA gives prefix + O-flag; hosts SLAAC addresses and fetch DNS via DHCPv6. 'IPv6 addressing without state' → SLAAC + stateless DHCPv6.

pitfalls: Expecting DHCPv6 to work like v4 — no broadcast, different model.
M/O flags wrong — hosts get addresses but no DNS (or vice versa).
No RA guard — rogue RAs hijack IPv6 on the LAN.
lessons.try_it: Capture RAs and verify the M/O flags match your design.

lessons.title: 802.1Q Trunking and DTP
concepts: 802.1Q tags frames with a 4-byte VLAN ID (12 bits = 4096 VLANs); native VLAN crosses untagged and must match both ends.
DTP negotiates trunking: dynamic auto/desirable can form trunks automatically — disable with 'switchport mode access' + 'switchport nonegotiate' on host ports.
Allowed VLAN list prunes unnecessary broadcasts: 'switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30'.
VLAN hopping attacks exploit DTP/auto-trunking — harden every access port.

example.code:
Switch(config)# interface gi0/1
Switch(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
Switch(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 99
Switch(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30
! harden host ports:
Switch(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
Switch(config-if-range)# switchport nonegotiate
Switch(config-if-range)# spanning-tree portfast
example.walkthrough: Trunk with pruned VLANs + native 99 (unused). Host ports: access mode, no DTP, portfast. This hardening trio answers most switch-security questions.

pitfalls: DTP left on host ports — VLAN hopping via negotiated trunk.
Native VLAN = user VLAN — double-tagging attacks; use an unused native VLAN.
Allowing all VLANs on every trunk — prune to reduce STP load and broadcast.
lessons.try_it: Configure a trunk, mismatch the native VLAN, and observe the CDP warning.

lessons.title: Port Security and DHCP Snooping
concepts: Port security limits MACs per port: static, sticky (learned then saved), or dynamic; violation modes: protect (drop), restrict (drop+log), shutdown (err-disable).
DHCP snooping builds a binding table (MAC/IP/port/VLAN) from trusted ports; untrusted DHCP offers dropped — kills rogue DHCP servers.
Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) uses the snooping table to validate ARP — stops ARP spoofing/MITM.
IP Source Guard extends to IP filtering per port. The trio (snooping+DAI+IPSG) is the access-layer security stack.

example.code:
Switch(config)# ip dhcp snooping
Switch(config)# ip dhcp snooping vlan 10
Switch(config-if)# ip dhcp snooping trust   ! uplink only
Switch(config-if)# switchport port-security
Switch(config-if)# switchport port-security maximum 2
Switch(config-if)# switchport port-security violation restrict
Switch(config-if)# switchport port-security mac-address sticky
example.walkthrough: Trust only uplinks for DHCP, sticky-learn host MACs, restrict on violation. 'Rogue DHCP on the LAN' → DHCP snooping.

pitfalls: Trusting host ports for DHCP — only uplinks to real servers are trusted.
Shutdown mode without errdisable recovery — one violation needs manual intervention.
Snooping without VLAN enablement — global + per-VLAN both required.
lessons.try_it: Plug a rogue DHCP server into an untrusted port and watch offers get dropped.

lessons.title: Wireless: WLC, APs, and 802.11
concepts: Architectures: autonomous APs vs lightweight APs + WLC (CAPWAP tunnels); cloud-managed (Meraki) alternative.
Bands: 2.4 GHz (long range, crowded, 3 non-overlapping ch 1/6/11) vs 5/6 GHz (more channels, shorter range); channel planning avoids CCI.
Security: WPA2-Enterprise (802.1X/RADIUS) for corporate, WPA3-SAE for personal; rogue AP detection/containment.
Roaming: same SSID/security across APs; 802.11r/k/v fast transition for voice.

example.code:
! WLC: WLAN -> Security -> Layer 2: WPA2 + 802.1X
! RADIUS server -> ISE/NPS for EAP-TLS auth
! RF profile: 5 GHz preferred, DCA channels, TPC power
show ap summary  |  show client summary
example.walkthrough: WPA2-Enterprise + RADIUS = per-user credentials, no shared PSK. 'Corporate Wi-Fi' → 802.1X/EAP-TLS, never WPA2-Personal.

pitfalls: WPA2-Personal for enterprise — shared key, no user attribution; use 802.1X.
2.4 GHz for dense deployments — co-channel interference; prefer 5 GHz.
No WLC redundancy — APs drop on controller failure; use HA pair/mobility.
lessons.try_it: Survey channels, pick 1/6/11 plan, and verify roaming with continuous ping.

lessons.title: Static Routing and Default Routes
concepts: Static routes: ip route <dest> <mask> <next-hop|exit-interface>; AD 1 (most trusted after connected); floating static (higher AD) = backup path.
Default route 0.0.0.0/0 points unknown traffic to the edge — every stub network needs one.
Next-hop IP (recursive lookup) vs exit interface (proxy ARP risk on multi-access); fully specified for NBMA.
Use for stub networks, single-homed branches, and precise control; dynamic protocols for larger/meshed topologies.

example.walkthrough: Specifics first, default last, floating static as backup. 'Simple branch with one exit' → static + default; 'backup link' → floating static with higher AD.

pitfalls: No default route on stub routers — internet-bound traffic dies locally.
Exit-interface only on Ethernet multi-access — ARP for every destination; use next-hop IP.
Forgetting return routes — routing must work both directions.
lessons.try_it: Build a 3-router triangle with statics, then add a floating backup and test failover.

lessons.title: EIGRP: Concepts and Tuning
concepts: EIGRP: Cisco's advanced distance-vector (DUAL algorithm); rapid convergence, unequal-cost load balancing (variance).
Metrics: bandwidth + delay by default (K-values); feasible successor = loop-free backup, precomputed.
Named mode (modern) vs classic; authentication (HMAC-SHA); stub routers limit query scope.
CCNA scope: concepts and basics — DUAL, successor/feasible successor, variance.

example.code:
router eigrp CORP
 address-family ipv4 autonomous-system 100
  network 10.0.0.0
  variance 2          ! unequal-cost load balancing
  passive-interface default
  no passive-interface Gi0/1
example.walkthrough: DUAL precomputes the feasible successor — link fails, backup is instant. 'Fast converging interior routing' → EIGRP with successors.

pitfalls: K-values mismatched — neighbors never form; leave defaults.
No stub at the edge — queries flood the WAN on flaps.
Variance without feasible successor — the backup path must satisfy the feasibility condition.
lessons.try_it: Break a primary link and watch the feasible successor take over.

lessons.title: BGP: Internet Routing Fundamentals
concepts: BGP: path-vector for the internet; eBGP between ASes, iBGP within; TCP 179; policies over metrics.
Path selection: weight → local-pref → AS-path length → origin → MED → eBGP over iBGP → router-ID.
eBGP multihop for loopbacks; next-hop handling; route reflectors avoid full mesh (CCNA: know they exist).
CCNA: single-homed/multihomed concepts, default routes, path selection order.

example.code:
router bgp 65001
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 remote-as 65002
 neighbor 203.0.113.1 description ISP-A
 network 192.0.2.0 mask 255.255.255.0
 ! influence inbound: as-path prepend; outbound: local-pref
example.walkthrough: BGP chooses by policy, not speed — local-pref steers outbound, AS-path prepend steers inbound. 'Control which ISP traffic uses' → BGP attributes.

pitfalls: Assuming BGP picks the fastest path — it picks by policy attributes.
Advertising without filtering — leak your full table, become transit accidentally.
iBGP without full mesh/reflectors — routes vanish silently.
lessons.try_it: Trace the path selection for one prefix through the attribute list.

lessons.title: DHCP: DORA and Relay
concepts: DORA: Discover (broadcast) → Offer → Request → ACK; lease time, renewal at 50% (T1), rebinding at 87.5% (T2).
DHCP relay (ip helper-address) forwards broadcasts to servers across routers — one server serves many subnets.
Bindings, exclusions (printers/servers), reservations (MAC→fixed IP); rogue servers blocked by DHCP snooping.
Options: 3 router, 6 DNS, 150 TFTP (phones), 43 vendor-specific.

example.code:
R1(config)# ip dhcp pool LAN
R1(config-dhcp)# network 192.168.1.0 255.255.255.0
R1(config-dhcp)# default-router 192.168.1.1
R1(config-dhcp)# dns-server 8.8.8.8
R1(config-dhcp)# lease 8
R1(config)# ip dhcp excluded-address 192.168.1.1 192.168.1.10
! on the SVI facing clients: ip helper-address 10.0.0.5
example.walkthrough: Pool + exclusions + helper-address on client-facing interfaces. 'Clients get APIPA' → DHCP unreachable: check relay, scope exhaustion, snooping.

pitfalls: No helper-address on routed subnets — broadcasts never cross routers.
Scope exhaustion — no free leases looks like a server failure.
Excluding nothing — server hands the gateway's own IP to a client.
lessons.try_it: Exhaust a small scope and observe client behavior, then add exclusions.

lessons.title: NetFlow: Traffic Visibility
concepts: NetFlow/IPFIX exports flow records (5-tuple + bytes/packets/times) — who talked to whom, how much.
Flexible NetFlow: custom key fields; sampled on high-speed interfaces; export to a collector (SNMP is not this).
Use: capacity planning, anomaly detection, billing, forensics — 'top talkers' answers most questions.
NBAR complements with application classification.

example.code:
flow record v4
 match ipv4 source address
 match ipv4 destination address
 match transport source-port
 collect counter bytes long
!
interface Gi0/1
 ip flow monitor v4 input
example.walkthrough: Flows export to the collector; top-talkers report shows the bandwidth hog. 'Who is saturating the WAN?' → NetFlow.

pitfalls: Full NetFlow on core links — sample on high throughput.
No collector retention plan — flows are big data; age them out.
Expecting payload — flows are metadata, not packets.
lessons.try_it: Enable Flexible NetFlow on one interface and find its top talker.

lessons.title: SNMP: Monitoring Deep Dive
concepts: v3 is the only acceptable version: authPriv (SHA/AES), users not communities; v1/v2c send community strings in cleartext.
MIBs/OIDs: poll (GET) for metrics, traps/informs for events; informs are acknowledged.
Views limit what a user sees; engine IDs must be unique per device.
Use for device health (CPU/mem/interface counters); NetFlow for traffic, SNMP for health.

example.code:
snmp-server group NETOPS v3 priv
snmp-server user monitor NETOPS v3 auth sha AuthPass123 priv aes 256 PrivPass123
snmp-server host 10.0.0.50 version 3 priv monitor
snmp-server enable traps linkup linkdown
example.walkthrough: v3 user with authPriv, traps for link state. 'Monitor device health securely' → SNMPv3, never v2c.

pitfalls: v2c 'because monitoring tool defaults' — credentials in cleartext.
Polling every 30s for everything — poll smart, trap for events.
Duplicate engine IDs (cloned VMs) — traps misattribute.
lessons.try_it: Convert one device from v2c to v3 and verify traps arrive.

lessons.title: AAA: TACACS+ and RADIUS Design
concepts: TACACS+ (TCP 49): device admin — separates auth/authz/acct, encrypts whole payload; RADIUS (UDP 1812/13): network access (802.1X/VPN), encrypts password only.
Method lists: tacacs+ then local (fallback!); command authorization per privilege level.
ISE: policy server for 802.1X, profiling, posture; dead-server detection and fallback.
Local fallback account is mandatory — AAA server down must not lock you out.

example.code:
aaa new-model
tacacs server TACACS1
 address ipv4 10.0.0.10
 key SecretKey
!
aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local
 aaa authorization exec default group tacacs+ local
example.walkthrough: TACACS+ first, local fallback; exec authorization controls commands. 'Who did what on the routers?' → TACACS+ accounting.

pitfalls: No local fallback — AAA outage = locked out of every device.
RADIUS for device admin — wrong tool; TACACS+ separates command authz.
Shared keys in cleartext configs — type-7 is obfuscation, not encryption.
lessons.try_it: Simulate AAA failure and verify local fallback login.

lessons.title: DMVPN: Dynamic Multipoint VPN
concepts: Hub-and-spoke that builds spoke-to-spoke tunnels on demand: NHRP resolves NBMA addresses, mGRE carries many tunnels on one interface.
Phases: 1 = hub-only forwarding, 2 = spoke-to-spoke (summaries), 3 = NHRP redirect/shortcut (best scaling).
IPsec protects all tunnels; routing (EIGRP/OSPF/BGP) runs over the tunnel interfaces.
Use for large branch rollouts where full mesh is unmanageable.

example.code:
! Hub:
interface Tunnel0
 ip address 10.255.0.1 255.255.255.0
 tunnel source Gi0/0
 tunnel mode gre multipoint
 ip nhrp network-id 1
 ip nhrp map multicast dynamic
example.walkthrough: Spokes register with NHRP; Phase 3 builds direct spoke tunnels. '100 branches, dynamic mesh' → DMVPN Phase 3.

pitfalls: Phase 1 for large scale — all traffic hairpins the hub.
NHRP auth missing — spoofed registrations hijack tunnels.
MTU/fragmentation — GRE+IPsec overhead breaks PMTUD; adjust TCP MSS.
lessons.try_it: Show NHRP mappings and verify a spoke-to-spoke shortcut.

lessons.title: Config Management and Archiving
concepts: Archive configs automatically: 'archive' with SCP/TFTP path, 'write-memory' triggers, rollback via 'configure replace'.
Config diff: 'show archive config differences' before/after changes.
Change control: archive on every write + syslog; periodic snapshots for drift detection.
Golden configs + compliance checks catch drift before audits do.

example.code:
archive
 path scp://backup@10.0.0.50/$h-$t
 write-memory
 time-period 1440
! rollback:
configure replace scp://backup@10.0.0.50/router1-20261010 force
example.walkthrough: Every write-memory archives; bad change → configure replace rolls back. 'Undo last night's change' → archive + configure replace.

pitfalls: Manual backups only — the one time you forget is the outage.
TFTP for configs — credentials/configs in cleartext; use SCP.
No diff before change windows — you cannot prove what changed.
lessons.try_it: Archive, make a change, diff, then roll back.

lessons.title: How to Use This Bootcamp
concepts: The study order is deliberate — follow it: Start Here (this domain: how to study, Cisco CCNA exam structure) → Lessons (deep-dives in domain order: Network Fundamentals, Network Access, IP Connectivity, IP Services, Security Fundamentals, Automation & Programmability) → Scenarios (multiple-choice drills, untimed, with full explanations) → Labs (hands-on terminal exercises) → Timed mock (the full 200-301 simulation). Each layer assumes the one before.

What 'terminal' means: a terminal (also called console or shell) is a text window where you type commands and the computer prints results — no buttons, no mouse. Cloud CLIs (aws, az) follow the same pattern: service, then action, then flags. You cannot break anything by typing a wrong command in the labs — the worst case is an error message, which is itself information.

The 200-301 exam strategy baked into this bootcamp: learn the concept in Lessons, recognize it in Scenarios, execute it in Labs, then prove it under time pressure in the Mock. Skipping straight to the mock is like taking the final before the lectures.

How to read the drills: every scenario has a 'why' explanation naming the correct answer's letter. Wrong answers are designed around real misconceptions — read every explanation, especially for questions you got right by guessing.

example.code:
Week 1-2: Start Here + first 3 domains (lessons + scenarios)
Week 3-4: remaining domains + all labs
Week 5:   exam-strategy domain + timed mock runs
Exam day:  light review of pitfalls only — no new material

Suggested pace: 100-120 hours of focused study. Two 90-minute sessions beat one 3-hour slog.
example.walkthrough: Timebox each domain: lessons one day, scenarios the next, labs the third. The mock at the end measures readiness — 80%+ twice in a row means book the exam.

pitfalls: Binge-reading lessons without doing scenarios — recognition is a different skill from recall; the exam tests recognition under pressure.
Skipping labs because 'I know the CLI' — muscle memory fails under exam stress; the labs build it.
Taking the mock once, scoring 65%, and booking the exam anyway — the mock is a gate, not a suggestion.
lessons.try_it: Open the first lesson of the first domain and complete its knowledge check right now.

lessons.title: 200-301 Exam Structure and Question Patterns
concepts: The 200-301 exam is multiple-choice and multiple-response, delivered at a testing center or via online proctoring. Questions are scenario-based: a paragraph of context, then 'what should you do?' — never pure trivia.

Every question has one best answer and three distractors built from common misconceptions. Two answers often look right; the correct one matches the constraint words: 'most cost-effective,' 'least operational overhead,' 'most secure,' 'highly available.'
Cisco exams test decision-making, not memorization: expect 'a company needs X with constraints Y and Z' and four architectures. Your job is to map constraints to services.
Flag-and-return: answer what you know fast, flag the hard ones, return with remaining time. Unanswered questions score zero — never leave blanks.

example.code:
Question anatomy:
  Stem: 'A company runs ... The solution must be highly available
         and minimize operational overhead. What should the architect do?'
  Constraint words: HIGHLY AVAILABLE + MINIMIZE OPERATIONAL OVERHEAD
  -> eliminate self-managed options (operational overhead)
  -> eliminate single-AZ options (availability)
  -> pick the managed multi-AZ answer
example.walkthrough: Underline constraint words first, eliminate two distractors, then choose between the last two by re-reading the stem. This mechanical process beats 'gut feeling' consistently.

pitfalls: Answering from real-world habit instead of the exam's best practice — the exam wants the textbook answer, not your team's workaround.
Ignoring constraint words — 'cheapest' vs 'most resilient' flip the correct answer between the same two options.
Changing answers on review without new reasoning — first instincts, backed by elimination, are usually right.
lessons.try_it: Take 5 scenarios in the drills and write down the constraint words before answering.

lessons.title: Hands-On Labs: Building Muscle Memory
concepts: Labs are terminal exercises with automated checks: each step gives you a command to run, and checks verify the result. A hint appears if a check fails — read it, it diagnoses the exact miss.
The lab terminal is a safe sandbox: create, delete, break things. Every exam objective you can DO is one you will not forget under pressure.

For Cisco CCNA, the highest-value lab skills are the ones questions describe as actions: creating, configuring, verifying, troubleshooting. If a scenario says 'the engineer runs X,' you should have run X in a lab.
Repeat labs you fumble. The second run should take half the time — that speed delta is exam readiness.

example.code:
Lab loop:
  1. Read the objective (what 'done' looks like)
  2. Run each step, observing output (not just copy-paste)
  3. If a check fails, read the hint -- it names the exact gap
  4. Finish, then re-do the lab from memory tomorrow

  Checks are your examiner: green means you actually did it.
example.walkthrough: Do not copy-paste blindly: after each command, ask 'what did that change?' The checks only pass when the real state is correct.

pitfalls: Copy-pasting without reading output — the exam will ask what the output means.
Skipping the failed-check hints — they are the fastest diagnosis you will get anywhere.
Doing each lab once — spaced repetition (day 1, day 3, day 7) locks it in.
lessons.try_it: Complete any lab in the first domain, then redo it tomorrow without looking.

lessons.title: Study Plan and Readiness Gates
concepts: Phase 1 — Foundations (weeks 1-2): all lessons + scenarios for the first half of domains. Gate: 80%+ on each domain's scenarios untimed.
Phase 2 — Hands-on (weeks 3-4): all labs + remaining domains. Gate: every lab completed without hints.
Phase 3 — Pressure (week 5): exam-strategy domain, then full mock runs. Gate: two consecutive mock scores at or above 80%.
The two-mock rule is non-negotiable: one good score is luck, two is readiness. Book the exam only after clearing it.

example.code:
Readiness checklist:
  [ ] All domain scenarios >= 80% (untimed)
  [ ] All labs green without hints
  [ ] Mock #1 >= 80%
  [ ] Mock #2 >= 80% (different day)
  [ ] Can whiteboard each domain's core flow from memory
  --> Book the exam
example.walkthrough: Print this checklist. The exam costs real money and a failed attempt costs weeks — the gates protect both.

pitfalls: Booking before the gates — hope is not a study strategy.
Cramming new material the night before — review pitfalls and why-explanations only.
Ignoring weak domains — the exam weights them; your plan must too.
lessons.try_it: Score yourself against the checklist right now and date your exam only when it is green.

lessons.title: Capstone: Branch Office Network Build — Plan
concepts: Your capstone proves Cisco CCNA skills end-to-end: a complete branch network: VLANs + STP + EtherChannel access layer, OSPF to HQ over IPsec VTI, DHCP/DNS services, hardened devices, and automated config management
Plan before building: define success criteria (what 'done' looks like), list every service/resource, and sequence the build so each step is verifiable.
Document as you go: architecture diagram, decisions and tradeoffs, costs. Hiring managers and examiners both grade the trail, not just the result.
Scope control: the capstone must be finishable in a weekend. Cut nice-to-haves ruthlessly; depth on core objectives beats breadth.

example.code:
Project: Branch Office Network Build
  Milestone 1: Access: 3 VLANs (data/voice/guest), 802.1Q trunks, RSTP with deterministic root, LACP uplinks
  Milestone 2: Routing: OSPF area 0 to HQ, HSRP gateway redundancy, static default with floating backup
  Milestone 3: Services: DHCP pools + relay, NAT/PAT for internet, NTP hierarchy
  Milestone 4: Security: port security + DHCP snooping + DAI, extended ACLs, SSH-only management with TACACS+
  Milestone 5: Automation: Jinja2 templates, config backups, documented verification commands

Success criteria:
  [ ] All milestones deployed and verified
  [ ] Architecture diagram drawn
  [ ] Cost estimate documented
  [ ] Demo recorded or documented
example.walkthrough: Write the milestones on paper first. Each milestone ends with a verification command — if you cannot verify it, it is not done.

pitfalls: Building without milestones — 'almost done' for three weeks is not done.
No cost estimate — surprise bills kill momentum; estimate first.
Skipping documentation — undocumented work is invisible work.
lessons.try_it: Write your milestone list and success criteria before touching the console.

lessons.title: Capstone: Branch Office Network Build — Build
concepts: Build milestone by milestone, verifying each before moving on. Use infrastructure as code where the cert covers it — it is both the skill and the documentation.
When stuck: isolate (which milestone?), reproduce (smallest failing case), search error text exactly, timebox to 45 minutes then ask/document.
Security from the start: least-privilege roles, no public exposure unless required, encryption by default. Retrofitting security is 10x the work.
Tag everything (project=capstone, owner=you) so cleanup is one command and costs are visible.

example.code:
# Verify each milestone as you go:
# M1: resource exists and responds
# M2: integration works end-to-end
# M3: failure injection recovers automatically
# M4: costs match estimate
# Cleanup: delete stack / resource group when done
example.walkthrough: The build is the exam in real life: same services, same constraints, no multiple choice. Every lab in this bootcamp was rehearsal for this.

pitfalls: Clicking through the console with no record — you cannot reproduce or demo it later.
Leaving resources running — set a calendar reminder for cleanup day.
Skipping failure testing — 'it works' is not done; 'it recovers' is done.
lessons.try_it: Build milestone 1 today and verify it with the check commands.

lessons.title: Capstone: Branch Office Network Build — Present
concepts: Present like an interview: problem → constraints → architecture → tradeoffs → demo → costs → what you would do differently.
The architecture diagram is the centerpiece: data flow arrows, service names, and one sentence per major decision.
Quantify: latency, throughput, availability design, monthly cost. Numbers make the project real.
Map the project to 200-301 domains explicitly — this turns a project into exam evidence and interview stories.

example.code:
5-minute talk track:
  0:00 Problem and constraints (30s)
  0:30 Architecture walkthrough (2m)
  2:30 Live demo (1.5m)
  4:00 Tradeoffs + costs (45s)
  4:45 What I'd change (15s)
example.walkthrough: Record the demo even if shaky — a real recording beats a perfect slide deck. Link it on your resume and portfolio.

pitfalls: Demo without a backup — have screenshots/video in case live fails.
No cost slide — interviewers always ask; have the number ready.
Vague tradeoffs — 'I chose X over Y because...' shows engineering judgment.
lessons.try_it: Give the 5-minute talk to a friend or rubber duck today.

lessons.title: Reading Questions Like an Examiner
concepts: Examiners write distractors from real mistakes: the 'almost right' answer that misses one constraint, the 'real-world habit' answer that is not best practice, the 'correct service, wrong feature' answer.
Constraint words decide everything: 'MOST cost-effective,' 'LEAST operational overhead,' 'MOST secure,' 'WITHOUT managing servers,' 'MEET compliance.' Circle them before reading options.
Length is a signal, not noise: long stems hide the one sentence that matters. Read the last sentence first (the actual question), then scan for constraints.
Absolute words ('always,' 'never') are usually wrong; qualified words ('typically,' 'minimize') usually right — but verify against constraints, never as a sole rule.

example.code:
Stem: '...must retain logs for 7 years for compliance, with minimal
 effort. What is the MOST cost-effective solution?'
Parse: constraint = 7-YEAR RETENTION + MINIMAL EFFORT + CHEAPEST
Eliminate: manual pipelines (effort), hot storage for 7 years (cost)
Answer family: lifecycle to archive tier + retention policy
example.walkthrough: Practice this parse on every drill: constraints → eliminate two → decide between two. Speed comes from the mechanical habit.

pitfalls: Reading options before the stem — anchors you to attractive distractors.
Choosing the 'coolest' service instead of the constrained one — exam rewards boring and correct.
Overthinking 'trick' questions — most are straightforward constraint matches.
lessons.try_it: Do 10 scenarios writing only the constraint words first; check if your accuracy rises.

lessons.title: Elimination Tactics That Work
concepts: Two-pass method: pass 1 eliminates options violating any constraint (usually kills 2); pass 2 compares survivors on the remaining constraints.
Service-family elimination: if the stem needs serverless, eliminate every EC2/VM-based option immediately without reading further.
Cost-order elimination: when 'most cost-effective' appears, rank options by managed-ness — more managed usually wins unless a constraint forbids it.
Security-order elimination: when 'most secure,' prefer options with encryption by default, private networking, and least privilege — in that order.

example.code:
Q: '...serverless, lowest cost, event-driven image processing...'
A) EC2 fleet with cron        -> eliminate (not serverless)
B) Lambda + S3 events        -> keep
C) ECS on EC2                -> eliminate (not serverless)
D) Lambda + polling EC2      -> eliminate (polling = waste)
Answer: B in under 20 seconds.
example.walkthrough: Elimination turns 4-option questions into 2-option questions, doubling your odds even when unsure. Drill it until it is reflex.

pitfalls: Eliminating on vibes — every elimination needs a cited constraint from the stem.
Keeping an option because it 'sounds enterprise' — the exam does not grade vibes.
Forgetting to re-read the stem after elimination — the final two need the full context.
lessons.try_it: For the next 15 scenarios, write your two eliminations and reasons before choosing.

lessons.title: Time Management Under Pressure
concepts: Budget per question: total minutes ÷ question count, minus 15 minutes buffer. For a 130-minute, 65-question 200-301: ~1m45s each. A 3-minute question is stealing from two others.
The 90-second rule: if you have not eliminated two options in 90 seconds, flag and move on. Hard questions cluster — do not let one sink your pace.
First pass: answer everything you can in under 60 seconds. Second pass: flagged questions with fresh eyes. Third pass: review marked-for-review only.
Never leave blanks: with no penalty for wrong answers, a guess among two survivors is a 50% expected score vs 0% blank.

example.code:
65 questions, 130 minutes:
  Pass 1 (60 min): all sub-60s questions -> ~40 answered
  Pass 2 (40 min): flagged questions -> ~20 answered
  Pass 3 (15 min): review marked -> adjust a few
  Buffer (15 min):  breathing room / technical issues
example.walkthrough: Practice with the mock timer. Your pass-1 speed is the skill — the mock's per-question pacing feedback trains exactly this.

pitfalls: Perfectionism on question 7 — the exam is won on questions 30-65, which you never reach.
No flagging discipline — 'I'll remember to come back' fails under stress; flag explicitly.
Skipping the buffer — technical hiccups happen; plan for them.
lessons.try_it: Run a 20-question drill with a 35-minute timer and enforce the 90-second rule.

lessons.title: Scenario Questions: Multi-Service Design
concepts: Hard questions combine 2-3 services: identify each requirement, map it to a service, then check the combination for conflicts (regions, limits, auth).
Draw the data flow: source → processing → storage → consumer. Wrong answers usually break one arrow (wrong trigger, wrong permission, wrong region).
Permissions are the hidden test: the architecture can be perfect and still wrong if the role/policy is missing. Always ask 'who is allowed to call what?'
Cost and operations are tiebreakers: between two working designs, the exam prefers managed, serverless, and event-driven.

example.code:
Flow check for 'S3 upload -> process -> notify':
  S3 event notification -> Lambda? (permission: s3:Put -> lambda:Invoke?)
  Lambda -> DynamoDB? (execution role allows dynamodb:PutItem?)
  Lambda -> SNS? (role allows sns:Publish?)
  Dead-letter on failure? (SQS DLQ configured?)
  => 4 arrows, 4 permission checks. The distractor breaks exactly one.
example.walkthrough: For every design question, sketch the arrows and label the permission on each. The option with all arrows green is the answer.

pitfalls: Checking services but not permissions — the exam's favorite trap.
Forgetting DLQs/retries on async flows — 'what happens on failure' is always asked.
Regional mismatch — KMS keys, some services, and data residency are regional.
lessons.try_it: Take any 3-service scenario and draw the arrow diagram with permissions labeled.

lessons.title: Anatomy of Network Fundamentals: Tracing the Living Flow
concepts: Apply the four-step anatomy method to Network Fundamentals: (1) see the whole flow in context, (2) cut it open to reveal stages, (3) walk each step in sequence, (4) pull apart the handoffs and label them.
Every handoff in Network Fundamentals has a contract: what goes in, what comes out, what can fail. Map these contracts and you can troubleshoot anything in the domain.
The exam tests Network Fundamentals as flows, not facts: 'what happens when X fails at step 2?' Trace, do not memorize.
Narrate Network Fundamentals end-to-end out loud. If you cannot tell the story, you do not know the system yet.

example.code:
Network Fundamentals — living flow trace:
  Trigger: what starts the flow?
  Stage 1: first transformation (inputs -> outputs)
  Stage 2: handoff (contract between stages)
  Stage 3: final delivery (how do you verify?)
  Failure drill: break stage 2 -- what symptom appears downstream?
example.walkthrough: Pick the most important flow in this domain and trace it on a whiteboard, labeling every handoff contract.

pitfalls: Memorizing service names without the flows between them — the exam asks about the arrows.
Skipping failure drills — 'what breaks when' is the deepest test of understanding.
One static diagram — redraw it as a sequence; sequences reveal gaps.

simulations.title: VLAN 30 goes dark across the link
simulations.brief: Hosts in VLAN 30 on SW1 cannot reach hosts in VLAN 30 on SW2. VLAN 10 works fine across the same link. You have read-only show access on both switches. Work the evidence in order.

steps.symptom: VLAN 30 is down end-to-end between switches; VLAN 10 is fine.
evidence:
Port   Mode  Native vlan
Gi0/24 trunk  1
Vlans allowed: 10,20,30

Port   Mode  Native vlan
Gi0/24 trunk  1
Vlans allowed: 10,20
options: Reboot both switches — the trunk process is stuck
VLAN 30 is pruned from SW2's allowed list — add it with switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30
Change the native VLAN to 30 on both ends
Convert both ends to access ports in VLAN 30
steps.explain: The allowed-VLAN lists differ: SW2's trunk permits only 10 and 20, so VLAN 30 frames are dropped at SW2. Adding 30 to the allowed list (with 'add' so you don't wipe 10 and 20) restores it. Native VLAN and reboot are red herrings here.

steps.symptom: VLAN 30 now crosses the trunk, but one SW2 host in VLAN 30 still cannot reach SW1 hosts in VLAN 30.
evidence:
Name: Gi0/5
Administrative Mode: static access
Access Mode VLAN: 20
options: The host needs a new IP address
Gi0/5 is in the wrong VLAN — move it with switchport access vlan 30
Enable PortFast on the trunk
The trunk needs a native VLAN change
steps.explain: The host's port sits in VLAN 20, not 30 — a simple access-VLAN assignment error. Moving it to VLAN 30 puts the host in the right broadcast domain. Always verify the access port's VLAN when one host (not the whole VLAN) is isolated.

simulations.debrief: You practiced trunk troubleshooting in layers: allowed-VLAN pruning first (affects the whole VLAN), then the individual access port (affects one host).

simulations.title: The neighbor that never goes FULL
simulations.brief: R1 and R2 should be OSPF neighbors over 192.168.1.0/30, but routes from R2 never appear on R1. Work the evidence in order.

steps.symptom: No OSPF routes from R2 on R1.
evidence:
Neighbor ID  Pri  State        Dead Time  Address      Interface
2.2.2.2      1   EXSTART/BDR  00:00:33  192.168.1.2  Gi0/0
options: The router IDs conflict — change one
MTU mismatch stalls the database exchange in EXSTART — align the MTUs
OSPF is not enabled on R2 at all
The hello interval must be lowered to 1 second
steps.explain: Stuck in EXSTART with mismatched MTUs is the textbook signature: DBD packets sized for 9000 cannot be received on the 1500 interface, so the exchange never completes. Align the MTUs and the adjacency proceeds to FULL.

steps.symptom: After the MTU fix, the neighbor reaches FULL — but R1 still does not learn R2's 10.9.0.0/16 network.
evidence: R2: show run | section router ospf
options: Add network 10.9.0.0 0.0.255.255 area 0 on R2 so OSPF runs on those interfaces and advertises them
Increase the OSPF cost on R1
Configure a static route on R1 instead
Change R2's router-id
steps.explain: FULL adjacency only means the routers exchange databases — each router still only advertises networks its network statements cover. R2's statement matches only 192.168.1.0/30, so 10.9.0.0/16 is never injected. Adding the network statement with the correct wildcard mask fixes it.

simulations.debrief: You separated two distinct OSPF failure modes: adjacency formation (MTU) versus route advertisement (network statement coverage).

simulations.title: The office that lost the internet
simulations.brief: All 60 inside hosts lost internet access after a maintenance window. Inside-to-inside traffic works. Work the evidence in order.

steps.symptom: Inside hosts cannot reach the internet; LAN traffic is fine.
evidence:
Gi0/0 192.168.1.1 YES manual up up
Gi0/1 203.0.113.2 YES manual up up
options: The ISP is down — call the provider
NAT is producing zero translations — check the inside/outside designations and the NAT source rule
The default route is missing — add one
DHCP is down — restart the pool
steps.explain: Empty translations during active test traffic means NAT is not engaging at all — the first suspects are swapped or missing ip nat inside/outside and a missing or non-matching source rule. LAN traffic working rules out a general interface failure.

steps.symptom: The NAT rule exists, but translations are still zero.
evidence:
ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/1 overload
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip nat outside
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip nat inside
options: Add a second public IP for PAT
The inside/outside labels are swapped — Gi0/0 (LAN) must be inside and Gi0/1 (WAN) must be outside
Increase the NAT timeout
Change the ACL from 1 to 100
steps.explain: During maintenance someone swapped the designations: the LAN interface is labeled outside and the WAN interface inside, so return traffic logic inverts and no translations match. Swapping them back (Gi0/0 inside, Gi0/1 outside) restores PAT immediately.

simulations.debrief: You learned the NAT triage order: translations happening at all, then inside/outside correctness, then the ACL match.

consoleSims.title: Voice and data on floor 2
consoleSims.brief: Floor 2 gets IP phones with PCs daisy-chained behind them. Voice traffic belongs on VLAN 20 (named VOICE) so QoS can prioritize it. Gi1/0/20 and Gi1/0/21 are the two wall jacks — put both ports on the voice VLAN and save.
consoleSims.debrief: Separating voice and data into VLANs is how real networks prioritize phone traffic and keep broadcast chatter away from call quality. Same motion, twice — muscle memory is the point.

consoleSims.title: Overnight port move for Finance
consoleSims.brief: Finance moves to a new office overnight. Their PCs plug into Gi1/0/30 and must land on VLAN 40 (named FINANCE). The old uplink on Gi1/0/47 now feeds the new IDF closet, so it becomes a trunk. Do all three, then save — the morning crew arrives at 7.

tasks.hint: Type: write memory — no save, no change survives the next reboot.

consoleSims.debrief: Real changes chain VLAN creation, port assignment, trunk setup, and a save into one change window. Miss the save and the 7 a.m. power blip erases everything — CCNA simlets punish exactly that.

foundations.why_needed: CCNA is a subnetting exam wearing a networking costume: you will carve subnets, read wildcard masks, and validate addressing in your sleep. Refresher: an IPv4 address is 32 bits; the mask length (/n) fixes the network portion, leaving 32-n host bits; usable hosts = 2^(host bits) - 2 (network and broadcast are reserved). /24 = 255.255.255.0 (254 hosts), /25 = 255.255.255.128 (126), /26 = 255.255.255.192 (62), /27 = 255.255.255.224 (30), /28 = 255.255.255.240 (14), /30 = 255.255.255.252 (2, point-to-point links). Wildcard masks invert this: 0 = must match, 1 = ignore, so 0.0.0.255 pairs with /24 in OSPF network statements and ACLs.
